name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_1 - Acceleration due to gravity inside non uniform sphere

questiontext.text: The earth is an approximate sphere. If the interior contained matter which is not of the same density everywhere, then on the surface of the earth, the acceleration due to gravity

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The acceleration due to gravity at any location on or outside a mass distribution is determined by the gravitational field vector \(\mathbf{g} = -\nabla V\), where \(V\) is the gravitational potential resulting from the integrated contributions of all mass elements comprising the body.

Step 2: Direction and Magnitude Variations
When the interior of a spherical body possesses non-uniform density, spherical symmetry is broken. As a result, the gravitational field vector is generally not directed towards the geometric centre, and its magnitude varies across different locations on the surface.

Step 3: Impossibility of Zero Acceleration on the Surface
Consider a tangent plane to the surface of the sphere at any chosen surface point. Because the sphere is a convex geometry, all mass elements of the Earth lie strictly on one side of this tangent plane (within the interior half-space). Every volume element of mass exerts an attractive gravitational pull with a positive component directed along the inward normal to the surface. Integrating these inward normal components over the entire volume yields a non-zero, strictly positive inward acceleration. Consequently, the net gravitational field cannot vanish anywhere on the surface.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
On the surface of the Earth, the acceleration due to gravity cannot be zero at any point.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_2 - Motion of Mercury as observed from Earth

questiontext.text: As observed from earth, the sun appears to move in an approximate circular orbit. For the motion of another planet like mercury as observed from earth, this would

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dominant Gravitational Force in the Solar System
The Sun contains more than 99.8% of the total mass of the solar system. Hence, the primary gravitational force dictating the motion of any planet, including Mercury and Earth, is the central gravitational attraction exerted by the Sun.

Step 2: Apparent Motion of the Sun from Earth
Because Earth moves around the Sun in a nearly circular heliocentric orbit, the Sun appears to describe an approximately circular trajectory across the sky when viewed from the frame of reference of the Earth.

Step 3: Apparent Motion of Mercury from Earth
Mercury also revolves directly around the Sun in an inner heliocentric orbit under the Sun's dominant gravitational pull, rather than orbiting the Earth. Because Earth and Mercury revolve around the Sun with different orbital radii and different angular velocities, the relative position vector of Mercury with respect to Earth does not trace a simple circular orbit. Instead, it exhibits complex apparent looping and retrograde motions. This difference arises because the primary gravitational force governing Mercury's orbital acceleration is due to the Sun.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The apparent motion would not be circular because the major gravitational force on Mercury is due to the Sun.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_3 - Net gravitational torque on Earth due to Sun

questiontext.text: Different points in earth are at slightly different distances from the sun and hence experience different forces due to gravitation. For a rigid body, we know that if various forces act at various points in it, the resultant motion is as if a net force acts on the c.m. (centre of mass) causing translation and a net torque at the c.m. causing rotation around an axis through the c.m. For the earth-sun system (approximating the earth as a uniform density sphere)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Spherical Symmetry and Center of Mass
By Newton's shell theorem, a spherically symmetric mass distribution attracts and is attracted by external masses as if its entire mass were concentrated at its geometric centre. For a sphere of uniform density, the geometric centre coincides identically with the centre of mass.

Step 2: Line of Action of Resultant Force
Each infinitesimal mass element of the uniform Earth experiences a gravitational pull directed towards the Sun. Integrating these forces across the spherically symmetric body yields a resultant force whose line of action passes directly through the centre of mass of the Earth.

Step 3: Calculation of Torque
The net torque about the centre of mass is given by \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\), where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the position vector from the centre of mass to the point of application of the resultant force. Because the resultant gravitational force passes through the centre of mass, the moment arm is zero (\(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}\)). Therefore, the net gravitational torque acting about the centre of mass is zero.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
For the Earth-Sun system, treating the Earth as a sphere of uniform density, the net torque is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_4 - Orbital decay and falling of satellite debris

questiontext.text: Satellites orbiting the earth have finite life and sometimes debris of satellites fall to the earth. This is because,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Tenuous Atmosphere at Orbital Altitudes
Earth satellites orbit within the upper reaches of the atmosphere (thermosphere and exosphere). Although the air density is extremely low, it is not zero, and the high speed of the satellite produces a non-negligible atmospheric viscous drag force opposing its motion.

Step 2: Dissipation of Total Mechanical Energy
The total mechanical energy of a satellite of mass \(m\) in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) is negative: \(E = -\frac{G M m}{2r}\). As the satellite does work against the opposing viscous force, its total mechanical energy decreases (becomes more negative). Consequently, the orbital radius \(r\) must decrease, pulling the satellite into lower orbital altitudes.

Step 3: Atmospheric Re-entry
As the altitude decreases, the atmospheric density increases exponentially, causing the viscous drag to increase rapidly. This produces a progressive inward spiral, culminating in atmospheric re-entry where surviving debris falls to Earth.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The finite life of satellites and the fall of debris are caused by viscous forces that continuously dissipate energy, resulting in a gradual decrease in orbital height.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_5 - Nature of Moon orbit observed from Sun

questiontext.text: Both earth and moon are subject to the gravitational force of the sun. As observed from the sun, the orbit of the moon

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Criterion for an Elliptical Orbit
According to Kepler's first law and Newtonian mechanics, an orbiting body traces a strictly elliptical path only when it is acted upon by an inverse-square central force that is continuously directed towards a single fixed focal point.

Step 2: Gravitational Forces Acting on the Moon
The Moon experiences simultaneous gravitational attractions from both the Sun and the Earth. The total force vector acting on the Moon is:\[\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{Sun}} + \mathbf{F}_{\text{Earth}}\]

Step 3: Non-Central Nature of the Net Force
The vector \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{Sun}}\) is directed towards the Sun, whereas \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{Earth}}\) is directed towards the Earth. Because the Earth revolves around the Sun and does not coincide with it, the resultant force \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}}\) does not point directly towards the Sun at all times. Hence, the net gravitational force on the Moon is not a purely central force with respect to the Sun.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The orbit of the Moon as observed from the Sun will not be strictly elliptical because the total gravitational force acting on it is not central.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_6 - Orbital motion and Kepler laws for asteroids

questiontext.text: In our solar system, the inter-planetary region has chunks of matter (much smaller in size compared to planets) called asteroids. They

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Independence of Gravitational Acceleration from Body Mass
By Newton's universal law of gravitation, the force on a body of mass \(m\) located at distance \(r\) from the Sun of mass \(M_{\text{sun}}\) is \(F = \frac{G M_{\text{sun}} m}{r^2}\). The acceleration experienced by the body is \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{G M_{\text{sun}}}{r^2}\), which is completely independent of the mass of the body.

Step 2: Universal Applicability of Kepler's Laws
Because the orbital trajectory under a central inverse-square gravitational force depends exclusively on position and velocity—not on the mass of the orbiting body—any celestial object whose motion is dominated by the Sun's gravity follows an elliptical orbit governed by Kepler's laws.

Step 3: Motion of Asteroids
Asteroids revolve around the Sun primarily in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Even though their masses are small compared to planets, they experience the central gravitational field of the Sun and therefore describe closed elliptical orbits conforming to Kepler's three laws.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Asteroids move in orbits like planets and obey Kepler's laws.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_7 - Equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Inertial and Gravitational Mass
Inertial mass is a measure of the resistance of an object to acceleration under the influence of an applied external force (\(F = m_i a\)). Gravitational mass determines the magnitude of the gravitational attraction between the object and another mass (\(F = \frac{G M m_g}{r^2}\)).

Step 2: Experimental Equivalence
The equality of gravitational mass and inertial mass (\(m_i = m_g\)) is a well-established experimental fact verified to high precision by experiments such as those performed by Eötvös. Because \(m_i = m_g\), the acceleration due to gravity \(a = \left(\frac{m_g}{m_i}\right)\frac{G M}{R^2} = \frac{G M}{R^2}\) is identical for all objects at a given location on Earth.

Step 3: Independence from External Surroundings
Gravitational mass is an intrinsic property of a particle and does not depend on the presence of neighbouring masses, medium properties, or surroundings, exactly like inertial mass. Therefore, claiming that the gravitational mass of a particle depends on the presence of neighbouring heavy objects is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The statement asserting that the gravitational mass of a particle like a proton can depend on the presence of neighbouring heavy objects while the inertial mass cannot is false, making it the required incorrect statement.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_8 - Motion of small mass between two unequal masses

questiontext.text:
Particles of masses \(2M\), \(m\) and \(M\) are respectively at points \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) with \(AB = \frac{1}{2} (BC)\). \(m\) is much-much smaller than \(M\) and at time \(t = 0\), they are all at rest (Fig. 8.1).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Particles are arranged along a straight line at points \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) with masses \(m_A = 2M\), \(m_B = m\), and \(m_C = M\).
The distance relation is \(AB = \frac{1}{2}(BC)\). Let \(AB = r\); then \(BC = 2r\).
All particles are initially at rest at \(t = 0\), with \(m \ll M\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let the straight line define the x-axis, with point \(A\) situated to the left of \(B\) and point \(C\) to the right of \(B\). Attractive forces towards the left (towards \(A\)) are considered in the direction of mass \(2M\), while forces towards the right are towards mass \(M\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Newton's universal law of gravitation states that the attractive force between two point masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) separated by distance \(d\) is:\[F = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{d^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The gravitational force exerted on \(m\) by mass \(2M\) at \(A\) is directed to the left (towards \(A\)):\[F_A = \frac{G(2M)m}{(AB)^2} = \frac{2GMm}{r^2}\]The gravitational force exerted on \(m\) by mass \(M\) at \(C\) is directed to the right (towards \(C\)):\[F_C = \frac{G M m}{(BC)^2} = \frac{GMm}{(2r)^2} = \frac{GMm}{4r^2}\]Comparing the magnitudes:\[F_A = \frac{8}{4}\frac{GMm}{r^2}, \quad F_C = \frac{1}{4}\frac{GMm}{r^2}\]The net gravitational force acting on mass \(m\) is directed towards \(A\):\[F_{\text{net}} = F_A - F_C = \frac{7}{4}\frac{GMm}{r^2} > 0 \quad (\text{towards } 2M)\]Because the net force acts towards mass \(2M\), the particle of mass \(m\) accelerates and moves towards \(2M\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
As \(m\) moves towards \(A\), distance \(r\) decreases, causing the attraction towards \(2M\) to grow even stronger than that towards \(M\). Thus, \(m\) will move towards \(2M\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_9 - Variation of acceleration due to gravity

questiontext.text: Which of the following options are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Variation with Altitude
At height \(h\) above the surface of the Earth, the acceleration due to gravity is given by \(g(h) = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}\). Because the denominator increases with height, the acceleration due to gravity decreases with increasing altitude.

Step 2: Variation with Depth
Inside a uniform solid spherical Earth of radius \(R\) and mass \(M\), the acceleration due to gravity at depth \(d\) from the surface is \(g(d) = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)\). As depth \(d\) increases, the term \(\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)\) decreases, reaching zero at the centre. Therefore, acceleration due to gravity decreases, rather than increases, with depth.

Step 3: Variation with Latitude
Due to the Earth's rotation with angular speed \(\omega\), the apparent acceleration due to gravity at latitude \(\lambda\) is given by \(g_\lambda = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\lambda\). As latitude increases from the equator (\(\lambda = 0^\circ\)) towards the poles (\(\lambda = 90^\circ\)), \(\cos\lambda\) decreases towards zero, causing the centrifugal deduction to diminish. Consequently, the acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing latitude.

Step 4: Dependence on Earth's Mass
The value of surface gravity is \(g = \frac{GM}{R^2}\), which is directly proportional to the mass of the Earth \(M\). Hence, it is not independent of the mass of the Earth.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that acceleration due to gravity decreases with increasing altitude and that acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing latitude.

answer.text: Acceleration due to gravity decreases with increasing altitude.
Acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing depth (assume the earth to be a sphere of uniform density).
Acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing latitude.
Acceleration due to gravity is independent of the mass of the earth.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_10 - Consequences of hypothetical inverse cube gravitation law

questiontext.text: If the law of gravitation, instead of being inverse-square law, becomes an inverse-cube law-

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Orbital Geometry and Bertrand's Theorem
According to Bertrand's theorem, stable closed bound orbits with non-precessing ellipses exist exclusively for central potentials proportional to \(r^2\) (Hooke's law) and \(r^{-1}\) (inverse-square force law). Under an inverse-cube law \(F \propto r^{-3}\), closed elliptical orbits are impossible.

Step 2: Instability of Circular Orbits
For an attractive force \(F(r) = \frac{C}{r^3}\), the effective potential for radial motion with angular momentum \(L\) is:\[V_{\text{eff}}(r) = -\frac{C}{2r^2} + \frac{L^2}{2m r^2} = \frac{L^2 - mC}{2m r^2}\]Because both the centrifugal barrier and the attractive potential scale identically as \(r^{-2}\), the effective potential lacks a local minimum. Consequently, circular orbits are strictly unstable, meaning any infinitesimal radial perturbation causes the body either to spiral inward to the origin or escape to infinity.

Step 3: Trajectory of a Stone Near Earth's Surface
For a small-scale projectile thrown near the Earth's surface, the vertical displacement \(h\) is negligible compared to the radius of the Earth (\(h \ll R\)). Over this localized region, the gravitational field is essentially constant and uniform in direction, resulting in an acceleration that is approximately constant. Therefore, the trajectory of a stone remains approximately parabolic.

Step 4: Gravitational Force Inside a Uniform Shell
Newton's shell theorem yielding zero field inside a uniform spherical shell is a mathematical consequence of the inverse-square law (Gauss's law in three dimensions). For an inverse-cube force, the gravitational forces from opposing surface elements do not cancel, so the gravitational force inside a uniform spherical shell is non-zero.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Under an inverse-cube law, planets will not have elliptic orbits, circular orbits are not possible, and projectile motion of a stone thrown near the Earth's surface will be approximately parabolic.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_11 - Effects of ten times smaller Sun mass and larger G

questiontext.text: If the mass of sun were ten times smaller and gravitational constant \(G\) were ten times larger in magnitudes-

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Surface Gravity on Earth
Acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth is \(g = \frac{G M_E}{R_E^2}\). If the gravitational constant \(G\) becomes ten times larger while the mass and radius of the Earth remain unchanged, the surface gravity becomes \(g' = 10 g\). Thus, the acceleration due to gravity on Earth increases tenfold.

Step 2: Effect on Walking
The weight of an individual of mass \(m\) is \(W = mg\). Under a tenfold increase in \(g\), the downward force exerted by the body increases tenfold, requiring significantly greater muscular effort to lift the limbs and support body weight, making walking on the ground far more difficult.

Step 3: Effect on Raindrops
The terminal velocity of a spherical raindrop falling through air is given by Stokes' law balance: \(v_t = \frac{2 r^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 \eta}\), where \(\rho\) is the density of water, \(\sigma\) is the density of air, \(\eta\) is air viscosity, and \(r\) is droplet radius. Because terminal velocity is directly proportional to \(g\), raindrops will fall significantly faster.

Step 4: Effect on Airplane Travel
To maintain steady level flight, the aerodynamic lift \(L = \frac{1}{2} C_L \rho_{\text{air}} v^2 A\) must balance the airplane's weight \(W = mg\). With a tenfold increase in weight, the required lift increases tenfold, demanding an increase in flight speed by a factor of \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16\). Consequently, airplanes will have to travel much faster.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
With a tenfold increase in \(G\), walking on the ground would become more difficult, raindrops will fall much faster, and airplanes will have to travel much faster.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_12 - Planetary motion under opposite electrostatic charges

questiontext.text: If the sun and the planets carried huge amounts of opposite charges,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Superposition of Forces
The gravitational force between the Sun of mass \(M\) and a planet of mass \(m\) separated by distance \(r\) is \(F_g = \frac{GMm}{r^2}\). If the Sun carries positive charge \(+Q\) and the planet carries negative charge \(-q\), Coulomb's electrostatic force is attractive and also obeys the inverse-square law: \(F_e = \frac{kQq}{r^2}\).

Step 2: Central Inverse-Square Nature of Resultant Force
The total attractive force is:\[F_{\text{net}} = F_g + F_e = \frac{GMm + kQq}{r^2} = \frac{C}{r^2}\]where \(C = GMm + kQq\) is a constant for the given planet-Sun pair. Since this net force remains an attractive central force proportional to \(r^{-2}\), the governing equation of motion is identical in form to standard Newtonian gravitation.

Step 3: Verification of Kepler's Laws
1. Kepler's first law holds because any attractive inverse-square central force produces bound orbits that are ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
2. Kepler's second law holds because the force is strictly central, producing zero torque about the Sun, which ensures the conservation of angular momentum and a constant areal velocity.
3. Kepler's third law also remains valid in mathematical form, with \(T^2 \propto a^3\) for each planet under an inverse-square force law.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
All three of Kepler's laws would still be valid, which directly encompasses the statements that the first law remains valid and the second law does not change.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_13 - Long term planetary effects of decreasing gravitational constant

questiontext.text: There have been suggestions that the value of the gravitational constant \(G\) becomes smaller when considered over very large time period (in billions of years) in the future. If that happens, for our earth,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Orbital Energy and Equilibrium
For an orbiting body of mass \(m\) around the Sun of mass \(M\) at orbital radius \(r\), the balance between gravitational attraction and centripetal requirement is \(\frac{G M m}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r}\), with total mechanical energy \(E = -\frac{G M m}{2r}\).

Step 2: Effect of Gradually Diminishing Gravitational Strength
If \(G\) slowly decreases over billions of years, the gravitational attractive force binding the Earth to the Sun continuously weakens. Consequently, the orbital radius must steadily expand. Because the radius increases monotonically with time, the trajectory is an outward spiral rather than a closed, repeating ellipse.

Step 3: Eventual Escape from the Solar System
As the orbital radius expands, the Earth receives less solar irradiance, meaning the planet would become colder rather than hotter. Over a sufficiently long timeframe, as \(G\) continues to diminish, the binding energy tends to zero, allowing the Earth to unbind from the Sun's gravitational field and leave the solar system.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
If the gravitational constant decreases over very large periods, the Earth will go around the Sun in non-closed orbits and will eventually leave the solar system after a sufficiently long time.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_14 - Consequences of modified non linear mass gravitation law

questiontext.text:
Supposing Newton's law of gravitation for gravitation forces \(\mathbf{F}_1\) and \(\mathbf{F}_2\) between two masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) at positions \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\) read

\[\mathbf{F}_1 = -\mathbf{F}_2 = -\frac{\mathbf{r}_{12}}{r_{12}^3} G M_0^2 \left( \frac{m_1 m_2}{M_0^2} \right)^n\]

where \(M_0\) is a constant of dimension of mass, \(\mathbf{r}_{12} = \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2\) and \(n\) is a number. In such a case,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Acceleration due to Gravity
Let \(m_1 = M_E\) be the mass of the Earth and \(m_2 = m\) be the mass of an object near the surface. The magnitude of the gravitational force on the object is:\[F \propto (M_E m)^n \propto m^n\]The acceleration of the object is \(a = \frac{F}{m} \propto m^{n-1}\). For \(n \neq 1\), this acceleration depends on the mass \(m\) of the object, so acceleration due to gravity on Earth is different for different objects.

Step 2: Validity of Kepler's Laws
The force remains directed along \(\mathbf{r}_{12}\) and varies inversely with the square of the separation (\(r_{12}^{-2}\)). Because it is a central force, angular momentum is conserved and areal velocity remains constant, so Kepler's second law remains valid. The buoyant force acting on a submerged body is determined by the pressure gradient in the surrounding liquid: \(\frac{dP}{dz} = \rho_{\text{fluid}} g_{\text{fluid}}\). When \(n < 0\), the gravitational force per unit mass scales inversely with mass/density, reversing the typical buoyancy relationship. Consequently, a body lighter (less dense) than water experiences an downward net force and sinks.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The acceleration due to gravity on Earth will be different for different objects, only Kepler's third law will become invalid, and for negative values of \(n\), an object lighter than water will sink in water.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_15 - Direction of motion of polar and geostationary satellites

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dynamics of Geostationary Satellites
A geostationary satellite remains stationary relative to a point on the Earth's surface. Because the Earth rotates on its polar axis from west to east, the satellite's orbital plane must lie in the equatorial plane, and it must revolve in the same sense as the Earth's rotation—that is, from west to east—with an orbital period of 24 hours.

Step 2: Dynamics of Polar Satellites
A polar satellite travels in an orbit with an inclination of nearly \(90^\circ\) relative to the equatorial plane, passing over the North and South geographic poles. Its orbital trajectory therefore proceeds in a north-south direction, allowing it to scan successive strips of the Earth's surface as the planet rotates from west to east beneath it.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A polar satellite revolves around the Earth's poles in a north-south direction, and a geostationary satellite orbits around the Earth in a west-east direction.

answer.text: A polar satellite goes around the earth's pole in north-south direction.
A geostationary satellite goes around the earth in east-west direction.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_GRAVITATION_MCQ_Q8_16 - Proximity of centre of mass and centre of gravity

questiontext.text: The centre of mass of an extended body on the surface of the earth and its centre of gravity

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definitions
The centre of mass is the point determined purely by the spatial distribution of mass: \(\mathbf{R}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M}\int \mathbf{r}\,dm\). The centre of gravity is the point about which the net torque caused by gravitational forces is zero: \(\mathbf{R}_{\text{cg}} = \frac{\int \mathbf{r} g(\mathbf{r})\,dm}{\int g(\mathbf{r})\,dm}\).

Step 2: Condition for Coincidence
If the gravitational field \(\mathbf{g}\) is completely uniform in magnitude and direction across the entire volume of the body, \(g\) cancels out from the numerator and denominator, causing the centre of mass and the centre of gravity to coincide at the identical physical point.

Step 3: Evaluation for Real Objects on Earth's Surface
For everyday macroscopic objects of sizes less than 100 metres, the fractional variation in the Earth's gravitational field across the body is \(\frac{\Delta g}{g} \sim \frac{100\text{ m}}{6.4 \times 10^6\text{ m}} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\), which is negligible. Therefore, the centre of mass and the centre of gravity lie exceedingly close to each other for objects of sizes less than 100 m. Only for extremely large bodies (such as mountains or oceans) does the non-uniformity of the field produce an appreciable separation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The centre of mass and centre of gravity are close to each other for objects of sizes less than 100 m.
